analytic.title: Fixed Priority Scheduling with Deadlines Prior to Completion

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.head: Standard analysis for fixed priority scheduling assumes that all the computations for each task must be completed by the task's deadline. In practice this is rarely the case. The deadline is more correctly associated with the last observable event of the task, interval events and kernel overheads (such as the context switch away from the task) can occur after the deadline. New analysis is presented that caters for this situation. The result is enhanced schedulability without modiftcation to the preemptive behaviour of thp run-time system.
Introduction
div.p: The fundamental rate monotonic model is based upon a number of stringent assumptions. Since the initial analysis of Liu and Laylandlo in 1973 many of these assumptions have been removed (or at least weakened). For example: a tasks must be independentthe priority inheritance protocols'* allow tasks to share data that is protected by mutual exclusion; deadline must equal perioddeadline monotonic t h e ~r y ~. ~. ' can by applied if deadline ( 0 ) is less than period ( T ) , and arbitrary deadline a n a l y ~i s ' ~~~ can by used for the case of D > T ; tasks are periodic -hard sporadic tasks can by supported directly once the D=T requirement is relaxed3, and aperiodic tasks can be accommodated by various bandwidth preserving algorithm^'^, 6.

One further restriction is relaxed in this paper; namely that the deadline of each task occurs at the very end of its computationi.e. a task's worst case computation time, denoted by C , must always be completed by the deadline D .

In a recent report, Gerber and Hong7 argue that it is only meaningful to attach a deadline to the last observable event of a task. Moreover this last observable event may a a not be at the end of the task's execution, i.e. there may be a number of internal actions after the last output event.

When the model for analysis is enhanced to include kernel overheads5, it is necessary to "charge" to each task the cost of the context switch that allows it to preempt a lower priority task plus the cost of the context switch back to the preempted task once the higher priority task has completed. For realistic context switch times (i.e. not zero), it is meaningless to attach the "deadline" to the end of the context switch. Figure 1 gives a block representation of a task's execution (excluding preemptions for higher priority tasks). Phase a is the initial context switch to the task, phase b is the task's actual execution time up to the last observable event, phase c represents the internal actions of the task following the last observable event, and finally phase d is the cost of the context switch away from the task. The real deadline of the task is at the end of phase b.

div.head: Release Completion
div.p: Last Observable Event In the following discussions we shall denote by CD the computation time required by the real deadline (i.e. phases a + b only), and by CT the total computation time of the task in each period (i.e. all four phases). Note there is no requirement to complete C' by T as long as C D is completed by D . We assume throughout that preemptive priority based dispatching is being undertaken, tasks have unique priorities, tasks do not suspend themselves during their execution, and tasks are released as soon as they arrive (and hence they suffer no release jitter).

The rest of the report is organised as follows. In section 2 arbitrary deadline analysisI4 is reviewed. Section 3 then modifies this analysis to the case in which C D must be completed before D , but C T can, occasionally, run over T . This is the case examined by Gerber and Hong7. In section 4 we present an extended example. Finally in section 5 we present our conclusions.

div.head: Arbitrary Deadline Analysis
div.p: Utilisation based analysis is only really applicable to task sets that conform exactly to the rate monotonic model. div.head: Optimal Priority Assignment
div.p: Where deadlines can be greater than period there is no simple algorithm for calculating the optimal priority ordering; neither rate monotonic nor deadline monotonic assignment is optimal. This is also the case with the formulation discussed in this paper. To illustrate this, consider the simple two task system defined in Table 2.

div.head: Table 2: Priority Order Example
div.p: If task 1 is given the highest priority (because it has the shortest deadline) it will run for the first 4 ticks and task 2 will miss its first deadline. However the assignment of task 2 to the top priority level will allow all deadlines to be met.
Audsley has recently constructed an algorithm for assigning priorities when the simple models do not apply2. He formulates, and proves, the following theorem :

div.head: Theorem I f task k is feasible at the lowest priority level, then if the task set is feasible, there must exist a feasible priority ordering with task k at this lowest priority level.
div.p: By feasible we mean satisfy all deadlines in the worst case. If a task k is found then the problem becomes one of assigning priorities to the remaining task set. The theorem can then be reapplied, leading to an algorithm in which priorities are assigned in inverse order.

The following code in Ada implements the priority assignment algorithm; set is an array of tasks that is notionally ordered by priority set ( 1 ) being the highest priority, set (N) being the lowest. The procedure task-test tests to see whether task K is feasible at that place in the array. The double loop works by first swapping tasks into the lowest position until a feasible result is found, this task is then fixed at that position. The next priority position is then considered. If at any time the inner loop fails to find a feasible task the whole procedure is abandoned. Note that a concise algorithm is possible if an extra swap is undertaken. This algorithm is applicable to the model derived above. It is used in the following example.

div.p: Table 3 gives the details of the task set. Times are in units of 10 microseconds. Task 1 represents the overhead of the clock (i.e. period of lOms computation time of 2.5ms). The context switch away from another task costs lms (i.e. 100 time units). Task 11 and beyond have various amounts of computation after the last observable event. For example tasks 14 and 16 have considerable activity after their last output. These tasks are typical of those that take an input, produce an output and then undertake a detailed analysis of the input in order to add a correction factor to the next output (in the next period).

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Preemptive priority based scheduling is an effective implementation strategy for real-time systems. The role of schedulability analysis is to test whether a given task set will meet all its deadlines when executing under such a strategy. Various forms of this analysis all make the assumption that the deadline is concerned with the final computational event of the task. In practice this is rarely the case, the last observable event may precede some internal computations, and the context switch away from the task does not itself have a deadline.

The scheduling analysis may therefore fail a task set that, in practice, always meets all its timing requirements. In this paper we have presented new analysis that more accurately reflects true engineering needs. We have shown how all computation up to the final observable event can be guaranteed to be completed before a deadline even when the full amount of computation may extend beyond the deadline and even beyond the end of the period of the task. The result is a test that effectively enhances the schedulability of a processor without changing, in any way, the behaviour of the processor or its run-time environment.
